## Laboratory environment

Before designing processor datapaths and running machine code, you need a functional development environment. This course relies on three primary software components:

1. **Digital (by Helmut Neemann):** A modern digital circuit simulator used to design, simulate, and export our RV32I processor.
2. **RISC-V GNU Toolchain:** A cross-compiler (`gcc`, `as`, `ld`, `objdump`) that translates RISC-V assembly and C source code into bare-metal machine code.
3. **Python 3 & Automation Scripts:** Headless testing utilities and the hardware UART programmer tool.

You have two options for setting up your environment:

- **Option A (Recommended): VS Code Dev Container / Docker** — Fully automated, one-click environment with all compilers and tools preinstalled.
- **Option B: Native Local Installation** — Installing Java, Digital, and the RISC-V toolchain directly on Linux, macOS, or Windows.

## Dev Container (Recommended)

The course repository includes a ready-to-use Dev Container configuration. This ensures that toolchain versions, paths, and dependencies match exactly without interfering with your host system.

### Prerequisites

1. Install [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/) (Windows/macOS) or Docker Engine (Linux).
2. Install [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/).
3. Install the **Dev Containers** extension (`ms-vscode-remote.remote-containers`) in VS Code.

### Launching the Environment

1. Open the course repository folder in VS Code:
   ```bash
   code i2ca/
   ```

2. Press `Ctrl+Shift+P` (or `Cmd+Shift+P` on macOS) to open the Command Palette.
3. Type and select: **Dev Containers: Reopen in Container**.
4. VS Code will build the container image and mount your workspace. Once opened, all tools (`digital`, `riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc`, `python3`, `java`) are ready in the integrated terminal.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Open-Source Alternative: DevPod
If you prefer not using VS Code or want an open-source, client-only container launcher, you can use [DevPod](https://devpod.sh/). DevPod supports the same `.devcontainer` configuration, works with Docker or Podman, and integrates with other editors such as Neovim or JetBrains IDEs.
:::

## Native Installation

If you prefer running tools directly on your host operating system, follow the platform-specific steps below.

### 1. Java Runtime Environment (JRE)

Digital is written in Java and requires **Java 17 or Java 21**.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Linux (Ubuntu / Debian)
```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install default-jre-headless openjdk-21-jre
```
Verify the installation:
```bash
java -version
```

### macOS
Install OpenJDK using [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/):
```bash
brew install openjdk@21
```

### Windows
Download and install the **Temurin OpenJDK 21 (LTS)** installer from [Adoptium](https://adoptium.net/). Ensure the installer option *"Add to PATH"* is enabled.
:::

### 2. Helmut Neemann's Digital Simulator

1. Download the latest `Digital.jar` executable archive from the official GitHub releases:
   - [Helmut Neemann Digital Releases](https://github.com/hneemann/Digital/releases)
2. Place `Digital.jar` in an accessible directory (e.g. `~/Digital/Digital.jar` or `/opt/digital/Digital.jar`).
3. On Linux/macOS, you can create a convenient wrapper script in `/usr/local/bin/digital`:
   ```bash
   sudo mkdir -p /opt/digital
   sudo mv Digital.jar /opt/digital/Digital.jar
   cat << 'EOF' | sudo tee /usr/local/bin/digital > /dev/null
   #!/bin/sh
   exec java -jar /opt/digital/Digital.jar "$@"
   EOF
   sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/digital
   ```

4. Test running Digital:
   ```bash
   digital
   ```
   A graphical window with an empty digital canvas should appear.

### 3. RISC-V Bare-Metal GCC Toolchain

We use the 32-bit bare-metal RISC-V target (`-march=rv32i -mabi=ilp32`). Note that the 64-bit cross-compiler `riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc` includes full 32-bit compilation support when passing `-march=rv32i`.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Linux (Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04)
```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install gcc-riscv64-unknown-elf binutils-riscv64-unknown-elf
```

### macOS
Using Homebrew:
```bash
brew tap riscv-software-src/riscv
brew install riscv-gnu-toolchain
```

### Windows
Download the pre-built **xPack GNU RISC-V Embedded GCC** archive from [xPack Releases](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/riscv-none-elf-gcc-xpack/releases) and add its `bin/` directory to your system `PATH`.
:::

Verify the compiler:
```bash
riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc --version
```

### 4. Python Environment

The course automated verification and hardware flashing tools require **Python 3.10+** and `pyserial`.

Install dependencies from the course package:
```bash
pip install -r lab-package/requirements.txt
```

## Verifying the Toolchain

To confirm that your environment is fully operational, run these two quick sanity checks in your terminal:

### 1. Compile a RISC-V Assembly Instruction
```bash
echo "addi x1, x0, 42" | riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc -march=rv32i -mabi=ilp32 -c -x assembler - -o /tmp/test.o
riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump -d /tmp/test.o
```
You should see:
```text
Disassembly of section .text:

00000000 <.text>:
   0:	02a00093          	li	ra,42
```

### 2. Run the Headless Core Verifier Help
```bash
python3 lab-package/scripts/verify_core.py --help
```
You should see the verifier usage flags (`--circ`, `--cmem`, `--cycles`, `-v`).

## Repository Structure Tour

Before proceeding to Lab 1, familiarize yourself with the structure of `lab-package/`:

```text
lab-package/
├── hardware/
│   ├── digital/
│   │   ├── lib/                  # Predefined reusable subcircuits (regfile_rv.dig, extend.dig, CMEM.dig)
│   │   └── testbenches/          # Validation schematics (alu_testbench.dig)
│   ├── top_wrapper.v             # Nexys A7 FPGA top-level wrapper
│   └── nexys4ddr.xdc             # Pin constraints for Vivado
├── scripts/
│   ├── verify_core.py            # Automated headless core verification tool
│   ├── CoreVerifier.java         # Headless Java simulation engine for Digital
│   ├── flash_rv32.py             # USB-UART hardware programmer script
│   └── tests_rv32i/              # Official RV32I compliance machine-code tests (.hex, .s, .dump)
├── software/
│   ├── crt0.s                    # Bare-metal assembly startup code (Lab 6)
│   ├── link.ld                   # Linker script defining memory layout (Lab 6)
│   ├── main.c                    # C demo source code (Lab 6)
│   └── Makefile                  # Compilation recipes
└── requirements.txt              # Python dependencies (pyserial)
```

With your tools verified and the repository layout clear, you are ready to begin **Lab 1: From Gate to ALU**!
